entries.title: Mint Mobile Will Give You $500 Off Select New Phones When You Sign Up for a Year
entries.summary: The limited-time offer applies to the latest phones from Google and Samsung, but you must be a new customer who signs up for 12 months of the unlimited plan.
entries.content:
If you’re hoping to cut your cell phone bill by switching providers and maybe get a new device as a carrot, check out Mint Mobile right now. The popular budget carrier is offering a limited-time $500 discount on several new Android phones, including the Google Pixel 11 series and Samsung S26 series. To get the deal, you will need to sign up for a 12-month unlimited plan for $180, which breaks down to $15 a month (Mint requires full payment upfront, plus taxes and fees). Another catch? You have to be a new customer. Phones are only getting more expensive, so discounts like this are worth exploring.

Unfortunately, the list of phones is limited and doesn’t include Apple’s iPhones. On the bright side, the phones aren’t low-quality; in fact, many are on our recommended lists. The unlimited plan also throttles down speeds after 50 GB per month, but includes 20 GB for hotspot connections. Mint will offer an additional credit of $400 or more when you trade in an eligible unlocked phone (iPhone 16 or higher, Galaxy S25 or higher, Z Flip7 or Fold7 or higher, or Pixel 10 or higher).

Mint rarely offers deals or coupons because its plans are priced lower than traditional carriers, and you would have to pay full price for a new phone; while you’ll still have to shell out to cover the balance for the device, it is still more economical than the phone deals offered by the big carriers.

For more savings, check out the best Early Black Friday deals we are following.

Save Up to $500 on These Top Phones

The Google Pixel 11 is down to $399 (regularly $899) when you bundle it with the 12-month Mint unlimited plan, for a total of $579 (excluding taxes and fees). This makes the base model in the Pixel 11 series cheaper than the entry-level Pixel 10a.

Mint is also discounting the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL to $594 and $794, respectively (normally $1,099 and $1,299). All three Pixel 11 models are our pick for the smartest Android phones, combining great hardware, software, and Google’s Gemini AI. The Pixel 10a is our favorite Android phone overall, but unfortunately, Mint doesn’t offer it; otherwise, it could have been as low as $100!

Samsung fans will love that the flagship Galaxy S26 series (WIRED’s recommendation for the best flagship Android phones) is on Mint’s discounted phones list, as is the Z Fold8, the best folding phone. Mint is offering the S26 for $500 (regularly $1,000), S26+ for $700 (regularly $1,200), and S26 Ultra for $900 (regularly $1,400). A sub-$1,000 price for the Ultra flagship is a great deal, even when you add the one year of unlimited service for $180.

The Ultra is chock-full of features, including a built-in privacy screen that sounds gimmicky, but is surprisingly effective. With the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor, the S26-series phones are powerful devices. Samsung continues to improve on the camera systems, making them some of the best in the industry. We just wish Samsung would support the Qi2 magnetic system natively for wireless charging (they are Qi2-ready when you use a compatible case).

If you’ve been eyeing a foldable phone, Mint has the Z Fold8 for $1,700. This isn’t a big discount from the $1,900 regular price, but foldables aren’t cheap in general. On the Android side, this is our favorite foldable model, and it’s lightweight despite its large unfolded screen. It also offers great performance and battery life, but one downside is that it lacks a telephoto lens.

Motorola has its share of fans. If you’re one of them, Mint is discounting the Razr (our pick for the best cheap folding phone) and Moto G Play (an honorable mention in our best Motorola phones guide).

Mint is offering the Razr for $520, a savings of $180. Now, that’s not a deep cut, but it is one of the more affordable foldable phones to begin with; this deal makes it even more so. Despite the budget price, we found it capable, even if the performance and battery life aren’t as strong as the Razr Ultra’s.

If you don’t care about brand or performance and just want the best phone you can buy at the lowest price, check out the Moto G Play. Mint has it for $80 (normally $250). While it isn’t one of our top picks, it’s a capable phone for casual users. And at this price, it’s worth considering.

entries.title: Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang
entries.summary: Nvidia employees and tech insiders never thought the chip king would lose his job. Despite his sudden resignation, many of them are still in denial.
entries.content:
News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley—including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation, after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned.

As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave.

Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing.

“In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure.

Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company.

That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report.

Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate.

Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman.

On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.”

Huang’s resignation left them in shock.

The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure.

The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says.

Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week.

Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision.

Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer.

entries.title: The 10 Best Early Black Friday TV Deals (2026)
entries.summary: I found discounts of up to half off some of the top WIRED-tested TVs.
entries.content:
You should never buy a TV at full price. This is a hill I will die on, and I am proven right every year when I see 20-, 30-, and even 50-percent-off deals on some of the best TVs. It may be weeks away, but I'm already seeing some great Black Friday deals, especially on TVs.

If you're in the market for a new screen, now is a smart time to shop options of all sizes, from big, premium OLED TVs for a home theater to small art TVs for the bedroom. Because you'll be ahead of the deal-hunting masses, you probably won't have to worry about shipping delays or out-of-stock notifications. A WIRED reviewer has tried every TV featured below (with one exception, the LG C6, which is currently in testing).

For more great discounts, check out our guide to the best early Black Friday deals, as well as early discounts on mattresses, and espresso machines.

WIRED Featured Deals

  • The Best OLED TV Deal: LG C6 65-Inch OLED TV for $1,400 ($1,300 off)
  • The Best Budget TV Deal: TCL QM7L 65-Inch Mini-LED TV for $898 ($602 off)
  • The Best RGB TV Deal: LG Micro RGB Evo 75-Inch TV for $3,000 ($2,000 off)

Best OLED TV Deals

This is the lowest price I've ever seen for the 65-inch LG C6, a fantastic deal on an excellent OLED TV. LG's C-Series TVs are consistently among our favorites due to their high brightness, uniform blacks, and vivid, natural colors. Add in their ample connectivity, which makes them versatile enough for gamers, and it's clear why this is a top OLED pick.

The premium 2026 Samsung S95H OLED TV is now at its lowest price yet. WIRED reviewer John Brandon praised the TV for its accurate color and deep blacks. New to the latest S95H model is a silver bezel that’s recessed behind the main OLED panel, making the TV look like a metal picture frame.

I understand wanting a nice OLED TV but not wanting to pay premium OLED prices. That's where budget OLEDs like the LG B6 shine—especially when steeply discounted. The 48-inch version, in particular, is 50 percent off at Best Buy right now, which is such a good deal, I thought it was a typo. (I won’t be surprised if the price mysteriously goes up.) Brandon praised the TV's thin size, simple setup, and deep and rich blacks.

Best LED TV Deals

Spoiler for our upcoming review: This is one of the best midrange TVs available. It's a fantastic option that will satisfy most people, and at its current 40-percent-off price, it'll also satisfy most budgets. Reviewer Rick Broida was seriously impressed by its bright and vibrant color display, which has a distinct pop that’s a joy to behold.

This isn’t a huge discount, and I wouldn’t be surprised if the price went down closer to Black Friday. Even so, the TCL QM6K is one of the best TVs for most people, according to former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata, because of its well-rounded picture and reasonable price (even when not on sale).

Again, this isn’t the biggest discount I’ve seen for this TV, but 33 percent off is nothing to sneeze at for an already-good-value television. In his U7SG review, Waniata called this a near-premium model with a new-and-improved stand and an anti-reflective matte screen reminiscent of high-end Samsung models.

Best RGB TV Deals

The LG Micro RGB Evo takes the top spot in our guide to the best RGB TVs, and this is the lowest price I've ever seen it. Reviewer John Brandon thought movies and shows looked stunning and vivid on its screen, with highly customizable picture settings that put it in a league of its own. Keep in mind that it only comes in 75-, 86-, and 100-inch sizes.

Best Art TV Deals

The best art TV is Samsung's Frame Pro (2026) thanks to its excellent image quality, contrast, color depth, and anti-glare technology that far outshines the competition, says Brandon. The only problem is that it's historically been high-priced. While 17 percent off may not sound that impressive, it’s actually matching the Prime Day low I saw earlier this year for the same model.

This discount isn't as low as its Prime Day price (yet), but 50 percent off is still great and makes this budget-friendly art TV even more appealing—especially for secondary rooms. It's not as bright as Samsung's art TVs, but it does come with a far broader free art library, no subscription required.

Best Projector Deals

This is the best home theater projector we've tested, and it's at its lowest price to date. Yes, even at 25 percent off, this projector costs a pretty penny, but its dynamic, self-adjusting iris (which automatically increases or reduces light) puts it well above similar competitors. That, plus its outstanding brightness and contrast, means the picture quality is stellar even in broad daylight.

entries.title: Jensen Huang Is Out. Will Nvidia’s Rivals Cash In?
entries.summary: In a special episode of “Uncanny Valley,” we break down Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia, what comes next for the company, and where the AI industry goes from here.
entries.content:
Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang officially resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. He also faces reports of at least two more alleged affairs with Nvidia employees. In this bonus episode, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down how Nvidia’s board turned on its founder, what interim CEO Colette Kress means for the company, and how this moment could be a golden opportunity for Nvidia’s competitors.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO
  • Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim CEO
  • Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: We're bringing you an extra episode this week because Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang has officially resigned. His resignation caps a swift, stunning fall for the man who spent more than three decades building a company into the engine of the AI boom. We're going to talk about how a board known for deferring to its celebrity CEO finally changed its tune and who's going to be running Nvidia at least for now. Let's get started. Just for the room, we released a podcast this morning before this happened and then it happened. So now we're talking again.

Leah Feiger: I mean, who doesn't want multiple offerings from the Uncanny Valley crew, Brian?

Brian Barrett: It's true. Constant updates. We're going to do an hourly podcast from now on, just iterative, getting real in the weeds. No, how surprised is everybody that this happened? And I guess first, if you want some setup about what happened, you can listen to our previous episode, but I guess I'll first say really quickly, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was selling a lot of chips to, and then a report came out that he had another affair allegedly with someone who reported directly to him at Nvidia, and that feels like the final straw. So we're caught up. Are we surprised still?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, the first thing to say is the company does have rules on the books saying that you're not supposed to have a relationship with a direct report. And so when we talked and it was the Chinese spy, although that is the obviously more scandalous thing that has happened, it also really felt to me like Jensen was going to weather that storm. But then when the second affair came out, that felt like it gave the board a really good excuse if they needed one to say, "OK, we have to stop." And I think it's fair to say here that while there is no current reporting on additional affairs, I think the concern is if two have already come out, what if more continued to become public and they need to stop the bleeding?

Leah Feiger: But he still fought pretty hard to retain his role, right?

Zoë Schiffer: I don't think the board wanted him to resign. I don't think Jensen wanted to resign. I think that their backs were completely against the wall on this one. The company has already been through an incredibly embarrassing scandal that will drag out for the next many months as Jensen is dragged before the Senate and has to answer to people who have serious concerns about his advocacy for China and where the Nvidia chips have been going and all of that. Now there's a second affair again with a direct report and I think that the situation became very, very quickly untenable for everyone involved.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely. And now Nvidia has a new CEO in the name of CFO Colette Kress. Tell me about her.

Brian Barrett: Interim. So yeah, she'll be there for the time being, but she's been at Nvidia for a long time. She's been there since 2013, which means that she's worked closely with Jensen since before the company was the darling of the AI world back when it was a graphics processor for gaming laptops company. She was at Cisco and Microsoft before that. She's a real industry veteran. I think my understanding is she's really a classic CFO. I don't know if she's a long-term visionary leader of this company, but she knows Nvidia inside and out. And I think if you're looking for stability and you're looking for someone who's not going to create new drama and who's not going to have a scandal, that seems like she really fits that bill.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I think what they need right now is stability, like you said. They need someone to take the reins. They don't want anything else dramatic to happen to the company. And of course they're going to immediately kick off a search for a new visionary leader, which as we said in the last episode, there's not an obvious successor here. They've got to find someone who has incredible technical prowess, who has a real vision for where the AI industry is going and who will be able to learn Nvidia's business. I think it's doubtful that person ... Well, actually, I really should have learned from this experience that I shouldn't have hot takes. I was going to say, I don't think the person's going to come from—

Brian Barrett: No, keep doing it.

Zoë Schiffer: ... Nvidia internally, but what do we know at this point? It could be anything. So yeah, Colette will take the reins for the moment and the company needs to weather this storm and come out the other side.

Brian Barrett: And I think she does, as you might have guessed, she's going to be operating the business the way Jensen had, at least in terms of advocating for closer collaboration with China and the business lines that Nvidia has been going down, leaning more into CPUs recently, open source. I don't think you're going to expect anything other than business as usual. And when you have her in there, as we talked before, China is so important to Nvidia's future. Jensen Huang had lost all credibility on that point. So having someone in there who can make the case that, hey, we should have a better relationship with China, we should be able to sell more to China, who is not compromised in the way that Jensen has been, that's an upside. I mean, it's a lot of downside for Nvidia that Jensen's gone, but at least they can come into these conversations without that baggage. I think that's the main point here.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps even right the ship even slightly. I mean, with news of Jensen's departure, Nvidia's stock plunged, absolutely plunged, but one of Kress's big roles as CFO was communicating with Wall Street. So I'm assuming that there's a world where this could be slightly reassuring to investors perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I think so. The thing about the market, I guess, is that everything's always baked in. The market has already accounted for so much. So it did take a big plunge. I think as we're recording this, it had been stabilizing a little bit. I shouldn't say that because by the time this is out, it's going to go wildly in one direction or another.

Leah Feiger: It means it's a time for another emergency pod. We're just going to keep this going all day.

Brian Barrett: We're going to have to do another emergency pod. Exactly. All day. Get ready, folks.

Zoë Schiffer: We have been talking a lot though about how interconnected, not just the AI industry is, but the entire US economy, how tied up it is with just a few companies. And Nvidia really is, it's kind of Nvidia and Anthropic that so much of this is riding on. And so I think we have yet to see what the ramifications of this will be if Nvidia is able, like we said, to weather the storm, continue growing and leading the AI boom. It has been, perhaps it won't be dire, but so much of what has happened already has been completely unexpected for everyone involved so that I think there's a lot of uncertainty and instability that we still have yet to account for.

Leah Feiger: So from the politics side, I can see this very much impacting the White House's relationship with AI-related firms. I can just see this becoming a thing and we're going to continue reporting this out, but WIRED is keeping a very close eye on what this means for these relationships. Talk to me from the Silicon Valley side, what is going to get impacted here? Is it crazy to say that Anthropic's IPO could get tossed up in the storm? What are we really looking at?

Brian Barrett: No, so here's my thing. I'm not sure about the Anthropic IPO. I think, again, everything's priced in and I think they're going to do just fine. It'll still be worth whether it's $1.2 trillion or $1.4 trillion, whatever. It's going to be a huge IPO, one of the biggest history regardless of this. What I'm interested in is right now, people don't have many alternatives. Even if you wanted to separate yourself from Nvidia because of this scandal for some reason, you're not going to find something better out there for the most part. Some other companies have had some gains lately. So in the short term, I don't know. I don't think that this maybe changes that much. This will be one of the takes, much like Zoë writes her takes, I'm going to regret saying this. I think short term it doesn't do that much. I think longer term though, we've already seen a lot of companies investing in making their own silicon and making their own chips and finding ways to optimize their own sort of hardware stack against their software. I think of it the way that after everyone saw Apple making its own processors and having huge efficiency gains on the iPhone, companies started doing that within smartphone world. Everyone has their own sort of processor in the smartphone world. I think that's happening increasingly in the AI world, and I think that's long-term a threat, not to the industry, but to Nvidia itself. It comes at a time when other companies are really trying to find a path to do this without relying so much on Nvidia, and this is only going to accelerate that process.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I mean, but that was true regardless. This isn't a software moment. I think when Elon Musk took over X and suddenly people were fleeing the platform, you saw Meta kind of seize its moment and launch Threads in a few short months. You can't really do that with GPUs. Other companies have been trying to compete with Nvidia for years, and that competition has only heated up as the AI industry has become more and more powerful and there's more and more money to be had. But this is some of the most complex technology on the planet, and so you cannot just see an opportunity and turn it around really, really fast. It takes years of research and manufacturing. And so I think there already was this opportunity for other companies to come in and try and grab some of Nvidia's market share, and I'm sure they will try and capitalize on the moment, but it's not going to be as easy as other examples we've seen in recent history.

Brian Barrett: Oh, for sure. But I think it's more like if you're OpenAI and you're like, "I've been dabbling with making my own chips." I think then you go from dabbling to saying, "Oh, maybe there's more urgency here and I need to put more behind that." So I agree with you 100 percent. I just think it maybe accelerates and changes the way some people are thinking about how they go forward.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. And the people that are already doing it, I mean, is Lisa Su from AMD doing a victory lap right now? I assume that she's ordered balloons.

Zoë Schiffer: Isn't Jensen her cousin or something?

Brian Barrett: That's correct.

Zoë Schiffer: It's family drama.

Brian Barrett: Family drama.

Leah Feiger: That makes it even better.

Brian Barrett: Great Thanksgiving coming up.

Leah Feiger: Has this happened before, you guys? I mean, I know that CEOs have stepped down over in some ways less. The spy of it all makes it extra fun here. Have we built the entire US economy around the very horny behavior of a very powerful man?

Brian Barrett: I don't know if we built it around ... Yes? We've built it. I would say—

Leah Feiger: I'm asking the questions our listeners want to know.

Brian Barrett: I would tweak the sentence, we've built the economy around the behavior of a horny man, not around the horny behavior of a man. Does that make sense?

Zoë Schiffer: Wow, absolutely.

Brian Barrett: Just trying to diagram that.

Leah Feiger: All right. Good editing. Good editing.

Brian Barrett: I'm just trying to diagram that sentence a little bit out. I want to hear what Zoë has to say about this too. I think we talked about this a little bit yesterday where yes, so much of the economy relies on too few companies right now, Nvidia being the main sort of bulwark there, but also so interesting, I think we wouldn't have seen this at other companies in that other tech companies are set up where their CEOs are untouchable and Jensen is not. So Jensen owns 3.5 percent or so of Nvidia. The board can do this. If Mark Zuckerberg could do anything short of getting arrested and still be in charge of Meta, there's just no recourse. Elon will be in charge of his companies for as long as he wants. So I think there's the fact that there was even an opportunity for accountability here is in and of itself interesting in a way that's sad. You know what I mean? There should be accountability everywhere, but that's not how these companies are set up.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps that's why it's so shocking. We never get to see accountability in this manner and speed.

Brian Barrett: Yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I feel like there are examples of really unexpected departures or departures that were expected, but still came as a real shock. Even Steve Jobs, which it was known that he was very ill for a long time, but he was so synonymous with Apple and Apple's success before his death, and yet he had this really solid bench of potential executives who could come in and take his place, maybe not completely, maybe not with the total vision, but Apple would and did continue to grow. I think the moment that I think of more right now is Sam Altman's very brief and dramatic ouster from OpenAI, because that one like this, no one really saw coming. It was such a shock. It was so unexpected. There were a lot of questions as to why, but of course that took place over the course of essentially a single weekend where the board pushed him out. There were all of these background negotiations, and then ultimately he was able to come back and resume his role as CEO.

Leah Feiger: How long did that take? How long did righting that ship take? Are the stakes similar or different here?

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. Is OpenAI's ship righted? I think is the ...

Brian Barrett: That's a great question.

Zoë Schiffer: Sam Altman was able to come back. Obviously, he was able to remake the board with friendlier people, but I think that Anthropic has really continued to be pretty ascendant and pretty focused in the wake of that, what employees call the blip when Sam Altman left. Whereas OpenAI, it felt like has continued to spin out, have drama after drama and be a little less focused in comparison. I think Nvidia overall is a much more disciplined company. It's not like the AI labs. It has a typical corporate structure. It has very defined goals. It's been around for a lot longer. And so I think these are different and very significant ways.

Brian Barrett: Although Zoë, what they didn't have was a succession plan, right? I think Jensen pointedly, as of he did interviews within the last few weeks or month where he was like, "I'm going to be here for decades. I don't really need to have ... " Well, sort of proudly not worried about a succession plan and a structure that's so flat. We've talked about this before too, but he had 60 direct reports all up to him. So I think it is a little irresponsible maybe. Here we go. I think he probably had a fiduciary responsibility to shareholders to think a little bit harder about what happens if I'm not here. I think that there is sort of this sense of, "I'm the only person who can do this. I'll be here forever." And I see how that you'd need to have that attitude to be the CEO of the biggest company in the world or one of the biggest companies in the world. But the backside of that is we're going to find out if that's true really soon.

Zoë Schiffer: No, for sure. I mean, I think he's been leading this company for 30 years, and it seems like while we are not sure what the board knew when, certainly within Nvidia, there were whispers about these things happening. And like we talked about in the last episode, Jensen had an affair with a woman, a former TV journalist who was running basically a smuggling operation that by all accounts he should have known about.

Brian Barrett: Allegedly.

Zoë Schiffer: He should have known exactly what was going on there. And so I think if you have enough hubris that you can make those decisions and still feel completely untouchable, then it makes sense in that kind of twisted logic that you would also think like I don't need a successor because I'm untouchable. And in fact, that has proved to not be the case.

Brian Barrett: One thing we've been seeing in the lead up to this was Silicon Valley really vocally defending Jensen Huang and saying, "It's one mistake, it's no big deal." And then saying, "It's two mistakes. What's the problem?" And even this morning after the news happened, we're still seeing people say he's an irreplaceable icon. It's sort of like they're trying to take you have to separate the artist from the art kind of argument, but for CEOs, does that surprise anybody that they're still hanging onto this? And I guess I know how I feel. Is that a fair argument? Can you separate the artist from the art in a Silicon Valley big tech CEO context? Does that make any sense whatsoever?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, this is an area that Silicon Valley is very sensitive about. It's such a founder oriented environment here, and I think that Jensen is the founder of this business. He built this company from the ground up. He started it at a Denny's 30 years ago. So yeah, I think there is a lot of loyalty, not just to him, but to the idea that a founder is a unique type of person and that they bring something to the table that no one else can replace. I had conversations with people that really made me laugh where they would say, "Well, Jensen's irreplaceable and his biggest mistake was admitting the affair in writing." I was like, "Well, I do feel like the biggest mistake was having a relationship with the Chinese spy perhaps, but yeah, I hear you."

Leah Feiger: I also wonder how much this is, I don't know, even slightly a little bit of lip service. On the DC side, Trump has been voraciously defending Jensen, and yet we also know that there's machinations behind the scenes to figure out some sort of accountability measure in some kind, whether that's congressional hearings or other things that could be coming down the pipeline. Two things can be true at once. It's like what Brian said earlier, everyone's saying like, "Oh no, Jensen." And yet they're all ready to start building their own chips or figuring out how to diversify that pool.

Zoë Schiffer: And the interesting thing about a lot of these relationships is they are very transactional. I don't know if we're going to continue to see the types of defenses that we have seen so far, but this is a moment. I mean, the China hawks, this is their time. I feel like it's not conspiratorial to say in some ways they orchestrated this moment in so far as they were instrumental in getting the information out there. And so I think they're going to, I would assume, be using this moment to try and turn Trump more toward their side, to be more anti-China, to not have as many trade loopholes or what have you.

Leah Feiger: And Jensen has been the voice against that, in many times the only voice against that in the room. So I'm really curious to see how this plays out.

Brian Barrett: And Zoë, you've got your kids guesting on the pod, which is adorable, and again, another thing that I think should become a fixture. Thank you for doing this when you've got your hands full.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. They would love it. Yeah, they're in the laundry room right now watching Unicorn Academy. So this is honestly the best morning they've ever had in their lives, but ...

Brian Barrett: Love that for them. Love it for us. All right. Well, good luck to Colette Kress. Good luck to your 401(k), everybody. Thank you all for jumping on this emergency podcast.

Zoë Schiffer: Thank you.

Leah Feiger: Thanks all.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

entries.title: Walmart Early Black Friday Deals Double as Great Gifts (2026)
entries.summary: Save on some of our favorite giftable vacuums, headphones, pet gadgets, and more ahead of Black Friday.
entries.content:
The month of November is basically one big shopping holiday at this point, but I'm not complaining. Walmart is the latest retailer to officially launch its selection of early Black Friday deals and many of them happen to make great gifts for yourself or somebody else. Walmart+ members can shop select deals even earlier, while supplies last. We've gone through and highlighted the best discounts on WIRED-tested gifts below, and we'll keep this story updated through Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Walmart+ gets you free delivery on orders over $35, free shipping, access to Peacock or Paramount+, gas savings, and more. You can try it for 30 days for one dollar which may be worthwhile if you plan on doing some shopping at Walmart for the holidays; Just keep in mind that you'll want to manually cancel your membership if you decide it's not for you after 30 days, otherwise, it's $13 per month (or $98 per year). (Note that qualifying government assistance recipients can get this plan for 50 percent off.)

  • An excellent tracker: Apple AirTag (2nd Gen) for $23 ($6 off)
  • Almost all the tools you need: Workpro 408-Piece General Household Home Repair Tool Kit for $130 ($158 off)
  • The best automatic litter box: Petkit PuraMax 2 for $381 ($69 off)

Deals on Giftable Tech

This extremely portable power station is actually pretty easy to tote around, unlike some other gadgets we've tested in this category. Coming in at 17 pounds with a convenient grab handle on the back, it has a massive 768-watt-hour capacity and recharges in just over an hour. The port selection has everything they'll need to stay topped off on a camping trip or for a few days without power. If your prepper friend loves hoarding power banks, this will be greatly appreciated.

The Beats Solo 4 are a little older now, but in a world rife with noise-canceling earbuds and expensive over-ears, these still have a place. The on-ear cups are pretty comfy, especially if your giftee's noggin isn't too big, and they have the iconic Beats sound with a little less overt bass than their predecessors. They don't have noise cancelation, they don't automatically pause, and they aren't dust or water resistant. But for the right person, this price isn't bad. They might also be a good pick for teenagers that want cool over-ears.

We've seen this deal pretty consistently for this excellent Bluetooth tracker, which can add anything to your Apple Find My app. Use it to track down your luggage, your pets, your keys, or your wallet. I personally keep one in my car so I can remember where I parked it when I haven't moved it for a few days. The battery is replaceable and it has a built-in speaker so you can ping it to find it if needed. It would make a great gift for your scatterbrained friend.

Giftable Home Deals

Editor and handywoman extraordinaire Kat Merck says this is a “knockout deal” for everything you get. From pliers and screwdrivers to wrenches, bits, and a tape measure, it's hard to beat for an at-home tool kit. It comes with most of the non-power-tools you'd need for basic home projects. You'll probably still want a drill or other specialty tools, but this would make a great gift for a new renter (or for yourself if your tool kit currently consists of random Allen keys in a junk drawer).

This is a solid discount on the very best automatic litter box we've tried. It strikes a great balance between budget and features and should work well with most one- or two-cat households (provided your kitties aren't too oversize). It doesn't have AI or a camera inside, but it is easy to use, easy to keep clean, and it even sprays a deodorizing mist as needed to keep things smelling fresh. If your cat's litterbox is a source of marital strife, perhaps it's time to employ a robot.

We love this self-emptying cordless vacuum. It's efficient at cleaning (though works best on carpet) and has an auto-cleaning and auto-charging station. It's especially good for pet parents since it can convert into a hand vacuum and includes several attachments for detailed cleaning tasks. I'm at the point in my life where a vacuum is a genuinely exciting gift prospect; perhaps someone on your list is, too.

This adorable smart nesting box has an internal hygrometer and thermometer as well as two cameras (one interior, one exterior). It lets you witness the entire cycle of bird birth with an up-close and personal view of nesting parents. It's easy to set up and use, and while the app doesn't always identify everything correctly, it can still help you make sense of what you're seeing. And the built-in solar panel helps ensure that everything keeps operating with minimal input from you. Kat Merck says it makes an excellent gift.
